case_study_insert.main_stem: Ironhill Coffee Roasters (ICR) is a partnership between three partners in the speciality coffee roasting sector, employing a workforce of 16. Founded in 2015 by Petra Lindqvist and Sam Okafor, the business roasts single-origin beans for independent cafés and sells branded retail bags online and in store, and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. ICR plans to invest $260,000 in a second roastery unit, financed by a $120,000 bank loan and $140,000 partners' capital contributions. It has fixed costs of $141,000 a year, a variable cost of $11.80 a unit and a selling price of $16.50, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. ICR faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 8% on packing shifts, and its roasting defect rate has risen to 2.1%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — August 2026: A survey of 400 independent café owners found that 63% would stock Ironhill single-origin bags, 57% want weekly delivery, and 48% would pay up to $1.00 more per bag for fully traceable lots. The roasting log shows output of 1,900 kg a week, a defect rate of 2.1% and average order fulfilment of 2 days. Customer complaints fell from 18 to 9 per month. ICR plans a quality assurance pilot with its two largest café accounts from January 2027. 5 of 16 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new drum roaster; off-the-job courses at the coffee institute cost $800 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Ironhill Coffee Roasters as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.5%, a move markets expect to hold through next year. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.5% from $12.60 to $13.42 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Green coffee bean costs have risen 15.6% year-on-year due to crop disease in key growing regions, coffee-price inflation is running at 10.5%, while consumer spending on speciality coffee grew 6.3% in the same period.

questions.question_text: ICR plans to finance its second roastery unit with a $120,000 bank loan and $140,000 partners' capital contributions. Explain two advantages for ICR of using partners' capital contributions instead of a larger bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Partners' capital contributions cost ICR no interest and no arrangement fees, which protects the partnership's cash flow at a time when it carries fixed costs of $141,000 a year and must absorb the 15.6% rise in green coffee bean costs. Every dollar of interest avoided shields the $16.50 selling price of the single-origin bags, helping ICR stay competitive with supermarket own-label speciality coffee while food-price and coffee inflation sit at 10.5%.

Point 2: Bringing in $140,000 from the three partners deepens their personal commitment to the second roastery unit and avoids pledging partners' homes or the roasting equipment as collateral for a bigger bank loan. In a partnership, unlimited personal liability already exists, but using retained partner funds preserves flexibility if the 15.6% bean-cost shock persists: the bank is not in a position to impose repayment terms or covenant breaches, and profit distribution can be adjusted by agreement among Petra Lindqvist, Sam Okafor and the third partner rather than to satisfy a lender's timetable — keeping democratic leadership workable during the build-out.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Ironhill Coffee Roasters, its partnership structure and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: ICR is launching its branded single-origin coffee bags. Consider café sampling roadshows, social media influencer marketing, or a loyalty card scheme with partner cafés. Which should ICR choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Café sampling roadshows: Travelling roasters and tasting sessions inside independent cafés let ICR demonstrate traceable, single-origin quality directly to the 63% of 400 surveyed café owners who would stock the bags, building owner advocacy at the point of sale. Costs are modest — a van, samples, a roaster and staff time — and tastings convert sceptical owners fast. Limitations: roadshows reach only the cafés visited, scale slowly across the country, and interrupt normal production with the same 16 staff, while travel and labour costs accumulate quickly per account signed.

Social media influencer marketing: Speciality-coffee influencers can reach thousands of home-brewing enthusiasts at low cost per engagement, driving online and in-store bag sales and explaining the $1.00 traceability premium the 48% of surveyed café owners would pay. It scales nationally, suits ICR's flat democratic marketing style, and content compounds over time. Downsides: conversion to wholesale café listings is indirect, influencer credibility varies, results are slower and harder to attribute, and creative demands time ICR's small team may lack.

Loyalty card scheme with partner cafés: A joint loyalty card giving regulars their ninth bag free (or partnered café points) drives repeat purchase, rewards the partner cafés that back ICR, and generates first-party data on drinking preferences. It is relatively cheap, measurable, and encourages weekly delivery patterns the 57% of café owners want. However, it only retains customers after first trial — it does not create awareness — and managing card logistics across dozens of independent cafés adds administrative load for a 16-person business.

Recommendation: ICR should choose social media influencer marketing, amplified by café sampling at two or three flagship accounts. Influencers create the national awareness and brand story that the $260,000 roastery launch needs, reaching both café owners and home drinkers affordably; sampling builds proof at the counter, but as a launch driver it is too slow and local to carry the campaign. Loyalty cards are rejected as a launch tool because retention mechanics matter only after awareness and trial exist — they should follow influencer-driven first sales, not precede them.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of ICR with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of ICR with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the sampling roadshows and loyalty scheme are rejected as the lead strategy.

questions.question_text: ICR operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. Explain two benefits for ICR of democratic leadership for its roasting and packing teams.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives ICR's 16 employees a voice in roast profiles, packing rotas and green-bean sourcing decisions, which raises motivation and ownership in a partnership business where staff see themselves as part of the craft. Employees who help set roast curves flag scorching or under-development early, attacking the 2.1% defect rate at source rather than through after-the-fact inspection — exactly what the planned quality assurance pilot with the two largest café accounts requires.

Point 2: Involving staff in decisions builds commitment and reduces absenteeism on packing shifts, where it has reached 8%. When operatives help design shift patterns around peak café delivery days (57% of owners want weekly delivery), attendance improves and cover gaps shrink without costly agency labour. Democratic consultation also strengthens the flat structure: fewer management layers means faster feedback from the roasting log to the partners, supporting the 2-day order fulfilment and keeping the 5 untrained staff engaged through the $800 coffee institute course rather than feeling imposed-upon.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ICR's democratic leadership, defect rate, absenteeism and cooperative-style partner culture.

questions.question_text: ICR is launching branded single-origin retail bags at scale. Consider batch production or flow production for the new bags. Which should ICR choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Batch production: Roasting and packing in batches preserves the single-origin, small-lot identity that independent cafés and home drinkers pay a premium for, allows ICR to switch origins (e.g. Ethiopian, Colombian) between batches, and limits unsold roasted stock in a volatile bean market. It supports traceability for the 48% of café owners willing to pay $1.00 more per bag for fully traceable lots, and quality control per batch is straightforward. The drawbacks are higher average unit setup costs, more cleaning/changeover downtime, and slower throughput — batch scheduling is stretched across 1,900 kg a week with 5 of 16 staff still untrained on the new drum roaster.

Flow production: A continuous roast-and-pack flow would maximise throughput, minimise handling between roaster and bagger, and lower unit costs through automation — appealing for winning national listings and supermarket own-label trials. Unit costs fall and consistency rises, important for the 2.1% defect target. However, flow production demands sustained high volume of one or two blends, large capital spend (impossible alongside the $260,000 second unit already financed by a $120,000 loan and $140,000 partner capital), rigid sequencing for any origin change, and would sacrifice the freshness window and the small-lot brand story that justify ICR's $16.50 price point.

Decision: ICR should choose batch production, at least for the launch phase. Batch fits the single-origin, traceable, premium brand the 63% of café owners already want to stock, matches the modest capital remaining after the second unit investment, and absorbs the 8% packing absenteeism with flexible scheduling. Flow production is rejected as the launch method because it forces volume before demand is proven, dilutes the craft positioning that underpins ICR's pricing power, and would over-commit the partnership's finances — though ICR can move one hero blend to a flow line later, once daily orders from the loyalty scheme and café contracts justify it.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of batch and flow production with limited application to ICR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both production options in the context of ICR's premium positioning.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both production methods in the context of ICR with a well-justified decision explaining why flow production is rejected for the launch.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how ICR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $141,000 ÷ ($16.50 − $11.80) = $141,000 ÷ $4.70 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16.50 − $11.80 = $4.70. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.70.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways ICR's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. ICR can compare the 30,000-unit break-even output with current output of 40,000 units to confirm a healthy margin of safety of 10,000 units, informing the partners whether the second roastery can be staged without breaching capacity or the $120,000 loan repayment schedule.
2. The contribution per unit of $4.70 lets ICR model the $1.00 traceability premium: if the 48% of café owners pay up, contribution rises to $5.70, and each extra 1,000 bags adds $5,700 toward fixed costs — quantifying the value of the QA pilot.
3. Knowing the 30,000-unit break-even lets the partners set minimum café order quantities and subscription thresholds for the retail bags, ensuring each account clears its variable cost plus a share of the $141,000 fixed costs before dispatch vans roll.
4. Managers can benchmark unit cost (average total cost = $141,000 ÷ 40,000 units + $11.80 = $15.33 a unit) quarter by quarter, trace the 2.1% defect rate back to drum-roaster settings, and decide whether to renegotiate the $11.80 variable cost in light of the 15.6% green coffee bean inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units. Working: contribution per unit is $16.50 − $11.80 = $4.70, and $141,000 ÷ $4.70 = 30,000 units. (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.70. This is what each single-origin retail bag contributes toward covering fixed costs after green beans, bags and roasting energy are paid. (iii) Four contextual uses explained: First, the partners can compare current output of 40,000 units with the 30,000-unit break-even to confirm a margin of safety of 10,000 units, giving comfort that the $260,000 second roastery can be staged without reckless demand assumptions. Second, the $4.70 contribution lets ICR price the QA-backed traceable lots precisely: a $1.00 premium lifts contribution to $5.70, so every 1,000 bags sold adds $5,700 toward fixed costs — a direct argument for the January 2027 quality assurance pilot. Third, break-even knowledge disciplines the café channel: ICR can set minimum weekly order sizes for the 400 surveyed café owners, ensuring each account clears its variable cost plus a fair share of the $141,000 fixed costs before weekly deliveries are locked in. Fourth, unit-cost benchmarking ($141,000 ÷ 40,000 units + $11.80 = $15.33 a unit) lets ICR trace the 2.1% defect rate to specific drum-roaster batches, judge whether the 15.6% green coffee bean inflation can be absorbed or passed on, and redesign roast schedules to protect the 2-day fulfilment promise before committing to the second unit.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ICR's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has ICR's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.28 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.38 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.61 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.82 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $65,000 inventories + $42,000 trade receivables + $18,000 cash = $125,000; 2025 current assets = $58,000 + $55,000 + $30,000 = $143,000. 2024 = $125,000 ÷ $98,000 = 1.28; 2025 = $143,000 ÷ $104,000 = 1.38. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($125,000 − $65,000) ÷ $98,000 = $60,000 ÷ $98,000 = 0.61; 2025 = ($143,000 − $58,000) ÷ $104,000 = $85,000 ÷ $104,000 = 0.82.

Evaluation: ICR's liquidity has improved meaningfully. The rise from 1.28 to 1.38 reflects cash growing from $18,000 to $30,000 and inventories falling from $65,000 to $58,000 — a healthier stock turn on fresh single-origin lots. The stock-independent measure rose from 0.61 to 0.82, still short of full cover, but moving in the right direction while ICR stages the $260,000 second roastery. The caution is trade receivables, up from $42,000 to $55,000 as wholesale café accounts stretch to weekly delivery and monthly settlement; if two or three larger cafés pay late, the 0.82 stock-independent cover could slip back below 0.70. Current liabilities also crept up from $98,000 to $104,000, so the partnership must keep disciplined control of supplier terms for green beans.

Conclusion: ICR's financial position has improved, but not yet to full short-term safety. The current ratio and especially the acid test ratio both strengthened, and the direction behind them (more cash, less stock) is the right one for an expansion year. However, the partnership should tighten café credit terms and keep a cash cushion while the second roastery is financed, because the improvement still leans on rising receivables that could reverse quickly.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether ICR's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ICR of introducing a quality assurance (QA) system for its roasting process.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A QA system builds quality into each stage — green bean intake, roast curve monitoring, resting and bagging — rather than inspecting bags after they are sealed, driving the 2.1% defect rate down toward the levels the two largest café accounts (on the January 2027 pilot) will demand. Prevention is cheaper than rework and waste, protects flavour consistency for the 400 surveyed café owners, and supports the $1.00 traceability premium the 48% would pay, strengthening ICR's claim to fully traceable single-origin lots and the supermarket listings the $260,000 roastery is designed to win.

Disadvantage: QA requires documented procedures, staff training on the new drum roaster for the 5 untrained employees, and ongoing auditing time from a 16-person workforce already stretched by the 8% packing absenteeism. The upfront cost — procedures development, recording systems, possible recalibration of the roaster and $800-per-head college courses — lands precisely when the partnership is financing a $260,000 second unit with a $120,000 bank loan. If checklists become bureaucratic, roasting flexibility and the fast 2-day order fulfilment suffer, and staff may see QA as box-ticking rather than craft, undermining the democratic culture that currently keeps quality pride high.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ICR's defect rate, QA pilot, training gap and expansion finances.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.5%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the 15.6% rise in green coffee bean costs will affect ICR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.5%): ICR carries a $120,000 bank loan on the $260,000 second roastery. A 0.5% rise adds about $600 a year to interest — trivial in cash terms, though it raises the cost of any top-up borrowing and signals tighter money markets for the partnership. Combined with the risk that premium speciality drinkers trade down, this is a manageable headwind, especially with $30,000 cash on hand and a 1.38 current ratio; locking the loan rate would neutralise it.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $13.42 per hour from April 2026): With 16 staff weighted to roasting, packing and delivery, the annual wage bill rises by roughly $1,400 per full-time worker at the floor rate, about $22,000–$25,000 across the team — meaningful for a partnership drawing profit distributions, but partial offsets exist: automation in the second unit, cross-training (reducing the 5 untrained), and productivity benchmarks (40,000 units ÷ 16 staff = 2,500 bags per worker per year). Democratic rostering can also hold morale while hours flex around café delivery peaks.

Input cost inflation (15.6% green coffee beans): Beans dominate the $11.80 variable cost per unit. A 15.6% rise adds roughly $1.10–$1.40 per bag; at 40,000 units that is about $44,000–$56,000 a year, dragging contribution from $4.70 toward $3.30–$3.60 and squeezing the partner distributions that fund their own living costs — before any renegotiation with café owners of the $16.50 bag price or the $1.00 traceability premium.

Conclusion: The 15.6% rise in green coffee bean costs will have the greatest impact. It strikes every bag ICR roasts, compounds on the same 40,000 units that carry the expansion's success, and cannot be fully passed on without risking the premium positioning; it also erodes both partners' and staff's real incomes at once. The wage rise is second; the interest rise is third and containable — but ICR must act on all three: forward-buy green bean contracts, lock the loan rate, and automate the second unit to hold unit costs and protect its $4.70 contribution.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to ICR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on ICR's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of ICR with a well-justified judgement that the 15.6% green coffee bean rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
